Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search Support Menu No early success for Moderna’s norovirus vaccine in phase 3 trial News brief August 3, 2026 Chris Dall, MA Topics Norovirus Adult (non-flu) Vaccines Share CDC / Alissa Eckert Vaccine maker Moderna said late last week that a phase 3 trial for its investigational mRNA norovirus vaccine candidate did not meet statistical criteria for early success. But the trial will continue. “The trial is ongoing and remains blinded as the Company works toward enrolling an additional cohort,” the company said in an update on its second quarter 2026 financial results. The phase 3 trial for mRNA-1403, a trivalent norovirus vaccine, launched in September 2024. The company aims to recruit up to 20,000 participants ages 60 years and older and an additional 5,000 aged 18 to 59 from countries in both the northern and southern hemispheres to assess the vaccine’s ability to protect against moderate to severe illness caused by norovirus. But the study has faced a clinical hold over a single case of Guillan-Barre syndrome and challenges with recruiting patients. According to reporting by Endpoint News, company officials said in a conference call that additional patients are needed because there haven’t been enough infections to adequately assess the efficacy of the vaccine. Norovirus is the leading cause of vomiting and diarrhea from acute gastroenteritis among Americans of all ages and causes 58% of all foodborne illnesses in the United States, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. An estimated 2,500 reported norovirus outbreaks occur in the United States each year. Ebola outbreak in DR Congo now second-deadliest in history News brief August 3, 2026 Stephanie Soucheray, MA Topics Ebola World Bank, Vincent Tremeau / Flickr cc The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is entering its third month as the second-deadliest in history and the largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the DRC. As of yesterday, DRC officials reported 3,695 cases and 1,623 deaths. The deadliest outbreak in history remains the 2014-2016 West African outbreak, which resulted in more than 11,000 deaths. The current outbreak is caused by a strain of Ebola virus, Bundibugyo, that has only caused three outbreaks in history and has no targeted therapeutics or vaccines. In a new Disease Outbreak News report from the World Health Organization (WHO), the agency says the outbreak is intensifying, and the crude case fatality ratio (CFR) now stands at 44%. Transmission rates are increasing, and in the last week of July, the highest weekly number of reported cases (567) and deaths (296) to date were recorded, the WHO said. There have been 151 cases among healthcare workers, including 44 deaths (CFR 29%). Outbreak affecting maternal mortality rates Ituri remains the most affected province, accounting for 88% of all confirmed cases and 82.6% of reported deaths nationwide. About 75.5% of case contacts are under active follow-up in Ituri. “A substantial scaling up of response activities is needed to get ahead of the outbreak,” the WHO warned. Today the Associated Press reported an increased maternal mortality rate in the outbreak regions, as women are skipping prenatal care and births attended to by medical professionals because of fears of contracting Ebola in medical centers. Noemi Dalmonte, deputy country representative of the United Nations Population Fund inthe DRC, told the AP that an average of six women a week were dying due to childbirth complications, double last year’s average. No link between MMR vaccination before age 2 and autism, large US study suggests News brief August 3, 2026 Meghan Holohan Topics Childhood Vaccines Measles Mumps Rubella Samara Heisz / iStock A national retrospective cohort study of more than 2.5 million children found no association between receiving the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine before age 2 years and having an autism diagnosis. “These results reinforce existing evidence supporting the safety of MMR vaccination,” wrote the authors, from the University of Washington. Some people worry that MMR vaccines cause autism, despite a lack of evidence supporting this theory. This paper is the latest to examine the MMR vaccine and autism by looking at the timing of the vaccine. Using the Cosmos electronic health record database, researchers looked at the records of more than 2.5 million children who had linked parent information from January 2015 through December 2024. The scientists followed the children until age 8 or their last doctor’s appointment before the study end date. Receiving the first MMR vaccine dose from ages 11.5 to 24 months was not associated with an increased likelihood of having an autism diagnosis. Kennedy acknowledges efficacy of MMR vaccine It’s been a record-breaking year in the United States for measles, with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reporting 2,371 cases this year, with 93% of these infections occurring in unvaccinated people. This is the highest number of measles cases since 1991. These results reinforce existing evidence supporting the safety of MMR vaccination. In an interview with CNN’s Dana Bash yesterday, Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said he is not responsible for the ongoing measles outbreak, despite years of saying childhood vaccines cause autism. “I’ve never questioned the efficacy of the MMR vaccine,” he said. Kennedy also encouraged parents to vaccinate their children. “A measles vaccine is effective,” he said. “It stops measles in about 97% of the cases.” In case you missed it Previous Next US adds 53 analysis.time: Published on August 3, 2026. Event date not specified in the evidence.
analysis.location_and_population: Global trial with participants aged 60 years and older (up to 20,000) and an additional 5,000 aged 18 to 59 from countries in both northern and southern hemispheres.
analysis.event: Moderna's phase 3 trial for its investigational mRNA norovirus vaccine candidate (mRNA-1403) did not meet statistical criteria for early success, but the trial will continue.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The trial aims to assess the vaccine's ability to protect against moderate to severe illness caused by norovirus. Norovirus is the leading cause of vomiting and diarrhea from acute gastroenteritis among Americans of all ages and causes 58% of all foodborne illnesses in the United States. An estimated 2,500 reported norovirus outbreaks occur in the United States each year.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The trial is ongoing and remains blinded as the company works toward enrolling an additional cohort. The study has faced a clinical hold over a single case of Guillan-Barre syndrome and challenges with recruiting patients. Additional patients are needed because there haven't been enough infections to adequately assess the efficacy of the vaccine.

analysis.brief_en: Moderna's phase 3 trial for its investigational mRNA norovirus vaccine candidate did not meet statistical criteria for early success, but the trial will continue. The trivalent vaccine, mRNA-1403, is being tested in a global study targeting up to 25,000 participants aged 18 and older to assess protection against moderate to severe norovirus illness. Despite challenges including a clinical hold due to a single Guillan-Barre syndrome case and recruitment difficulties, the company remains committed to the trial. Norovirus remains a significant public health concern, causing an estimated 2,500 outbreaks annually in the U.S. and accounting for 58% of foodborne illnesses. The trial's continuation underscores the ongoing effort to develop a vaccine against this highly contagious pathogen.

Despite challenges including a clinical hold due to a single Guillan-Barre syndrome case and recruitment difficulties, the company remains committed to the trial. Norovirus remains a significant public health concern, causing an estimated 2,500 outbreaks annually in the U.S. and accounting for 58% of foodborne illnesses. The trial's continuation underscores the ongoing effort to develop a vaccine against this highly contagious pathogen.

Full Release Longtime investor OPKO Health increases its position as Cocrystal advances toward norovirus Phase 1b data in late 2026 BOTHELL, Wash., Aug. 03, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Cocrystal Pharma, Inc. (Nasdaq: COCP) ("Cocrystal" or the "Company"), a biotechnology company developing novel antiviral therapeutics, today announced a $5 million investment from OPKO Health, Inc. (Nasdaq: OPK) (“OPKO”), a longtime investor in the Company, has increased its position through a $5 million investment as the Company advances its lead norovirus program toward Phase 1b topline data later this year. Under the terms of the agreement, Cocrystal sold 5,474,053 shares of its common stock to OPKO at a price per share of $0.9134, the Nasdaq Consolidated Bid Price on the trading day of closing, for proceeds to the Company of $5.0 million. No warrants or other derivative securities were included in the transaction. “OPKO’s increased investment reflects the confidence of one of our most steadfast supporters as we approach a defining moment for Cocrystal,” said James Sapirstein, Chief Executive Officer of Cocrystal Pharma. “We expect to report topline data from our Phase 1b norovirus trial by the end of the fourth quarter of 2026, and we’re grateful for OPKO’s continued conviction in the value of our lead asset, CDI-988, and our broader antiviral pipeline spanning influenza, coronaviruses and hepatitis C.” “As a longtime investor in Cocrystal, we’ve watched the Company build a differentiated antiviral platform with real clinical potential,” said Dr. Phillip Frost, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of OPKO Health and co-founder, director and principal stockholder of the Company. “This additional investment reflects our continued conviction in Cocrystal’s science and its path forward.” About the Offering The unregistered securities described above were offered in a private placement under Section 4(a)(2) of the Securities Act of 1933, as amended (the “Securities Act”), and Regulation D promulgated thereunder and have not been registered under the Securities Act, or applicable state securities laws. Accordingly, the unregistered shares may not be offered or sold in the United States except pursuant to an effective registration statement or an applicable exemption from the registration requirements of the Securities Act and such applicable state securities laws. About Cocrystal Pharma, Inc. Cocrystal Pharma, Inc. is a clinical stage biotechnology company discovering and developing novel antiviral therapeutics that target the replication of noroviruses, influenza viruses, coronaviruses (including SARS-CoV-2), and hepatitis C viruses. The Company’s lead program, CDI-988, is currently in a Phase 1b clinical trial for norovirus, with topline data expected in late 2026. Cocrystal employs unique structure-based technologies to create differentiated antiviral drug candidates. For more information, visit www.cocrystalpharma.com . About OPKO Health, Inc. OPKO is a multinational biopharmaceutical and diagnostics company that seeks to establish industry leading positions in large, rapidly growing markets by leveraging its discovery, development, and commercialization expertise and novel and proprietary technologies. For more information, visit www.opko.com . news.content_title: Fears over diarrhoea bug ruining summer holidays as vicious norovirus spikes 24% above ‘normal’
news.content: AS cases of norovirus remain high in the UK, fears grow over the vicious diarrhoea bug ruining summer holidays. Laboratory confirmed cases of norovirus are almost a quarter higher than the 5-year average, new data from the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has revealed. Cases of norovirus are currently 25 per cent higher than the five year average in England Credit: Getty The graph, from UKHSA, shows weekly norovirus laboratory reports in England during the 2026/2027 season, compared with the 5-season average Credit: Gov.uk The data also showed that rates of the vomiting bug were highest among children aged 0 to 4 years old. Norovirus is highly contagious and can spread through close contact with someone with the bug, as well as touching surfaces and objects that have the virus on and then touching your mouth. Sign up for the Health newsletter Thank you! UKHSA told Sun Health : “Rates are highest among children under four. We usually see the highest rates of reporting in this age group at this time of the year, so this is not unusual. “Parents and caregivers can help protect young children from norovirus by encouraging and supervising regular handwashing with soap and warm water, particularly after using the toilet and before eating. “Cleaning contaminated surfaces with bleach-based products can also help stop infections from spreading. Alcohol gels do not kill norovirus, so don’t rely on these alone.” Symptoms include diarrhoea, feeling and being sick, a high temperature, tummy pain and body aches. Norovirus reports over the last four weeks were 24 per cent higher than the 5-year average for the same four-week period, UKHSA said. It noted that reports of the illness – commonly known as the winter vomiting bug – have decreased in recent weeks and remain within the expected levels. But with summer holidays in full swing, Brits should still be aware of the potential threat. UKHSA explained: “Norovirus activity and the timing of the peak in reporting can vary considerably and differ from one season to the next. The bug causes vomiting and diarrhoea and is highly contagious Credit: Getty The graph shows norovirus laboratory reports per 100,000 in England during the 2026/2027 season, compared with the 5-season average Credit: Gov.uk “Since the 2019/2020 season, norovirus activity in England has been more variable compared to historical trends , likely due to multiple impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic .” So, what do you need to know about norovirus? The time between catching the virus and developing symptoms is usually between 12 to 48 hours. But it may feel as if symptoms have come on suddenly, UKHSA says. People are most infectious when showing symptoms, but it’s possible to pass on norovirus both before developing symptoms and after symptoms have stopped. Advice states that you should stay at home and avoid preparing food for others until 48 hours after symptoms have completely stopped. For most people, symptoms only tend to last for a short period of time with full recovery usually happening within two to three days. Some groups – including young children, the elderly or those with weakened immunity – are at risk of suffering a more serious and prolonged illness, however, which may require medical treatment. The NHS says that the most important thing for people with norovirus is to have lots of fluids to avoid dehydration. Young children, the elderly and those with weakened immunity could suffer more seriously from norovirus Credit: Getty What to know about norovirus... Norovirus, also called the winter vomiting bug, is a stomach bug that causes vomiting and diarrhoea. It can be very unpleasant, but usually gets better in about two days. Symptoms include: feeling sick being sick (vomiting) diarrhoea a high temperature a headache tummy pain body aches and pain Although it’s sometimes called the winter vomiting bug, you can get norovirus at any time of year. How is the bug spread: close contact with someone with norovirus touching surfaces or objects that have the virus on them, then touching your mouth eating food that’s been prepared or handled by someone with norovirus drinking unclean water or infected food Source: NHS And UKHSA told The Sun: “In most cases, norovirus symptoms will improve on their own within a few days. Parents should ensure children get plenty of rest and fluids to avoid dehydration. “If you are concerned about your child’s symptoms or they are becoming seriously unwell, seek medical advice. “If your child has diarrhoea and vomiting, keep them away from nursery, school or childcare settings until 48 hours after their symptoms have stopped. “If they are unwell, avoid visiting people in hospitals and care homes to prevent passing on the infection to those most vulnerable.” There is no specific treatment for the vomiting and diarrhoea bug and it cannot be treated with antibiotics – these work to fight bacteria, not viruses. According to UKHSA’s most recent data, cases of rotavirus – a viral infection causing vomiting and diarrhoea – were also higher than the five-year average. They were 7.2 per cent higher than the 5-season average for the same 4-week period, it said. It comes as an ‘explosive diarrhoea’ bug is tearing its way through the US, with, more than 6,700 cases confirmed through lab testing. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention noted, however, that it was aware of 11,500 additional cases requiring further investigation . And officials warned today that cases of cyclospora infections are also surging in the UK . So, if you’re travelling abroad soon, you may want to learn where the food poisoning holiday hotspots are and the precautions Brits must take to avoid getting sick

The study is ongoing, and a new group of volunteers is being enrolled for winter testing of the seasonal shot. Moderna's stock has nearly doubled this year, helped by enthusiasm for its cancer vaccine partnership with Merck. A Setback in the Race for a Norovirus Shot Moderna's norovirus vaccine has hit a roadblock. On July 31, the company said its Phase 3 trial of the mRNA candidate for the gastrointestinal virus did not achieve the early success criteria. Moderna emphasized that the study is continuing. On a conference call, executives said they are adding another group of volunteers to evaluate the seasonal vaccine during the winter. The norovirus program is part of Moderna's larger strategy to depend less on the Covid shot. Moderna expects the Food and Drug Administration to rule on its mRNA-based flu vaccine by Aug. 5. A green light would open the door for a combined flu-Covid shot to reach the U.S. market. The public disagreement with regulators highlighted how politically charged mRNA technology has become. In June, FDA advisers voted unanimously in favor of the vaccine. The agency is not required to follow their advice, but it generally does. What It Means for Your Portfolio Upcoming catalysts for Moderna include a decision on the flu vaccine by Aug. 5, possible late-stage melanoma data this year, and winter testing of its norovirus shot. Moderna is trying to build a broader franchise beyond Covid, and these events are part of that goal. An approved flu shot would add a second product in the U.S., while a successful norovirus vaccine could also become a seasonal offering. The cancer collaboration with Merck represents a completely different market from infectious disease, which is why investors have watched it closely. The company's plan depends on these programs advancing. If the norovirus shot succeeds in winter testing, Moderna would have another seasonal product beyond flu and Covid, reducing its reliance on the Covid vaccine. The Merck partnership likewise gives investors a reason to view Moderna as more than a one-vaccine company. Moderna still has several key events on the horizon for investors. Moderna's shares have already nearly doubled this year, helped by enthusiasm for its cancer vaccine partnership with Merck, but the company still needs to broaden beyond Covid. analysis.time: Publication date: July 31, 2026. Event date: July 31, 2026 (Phase 3 trial results announcement).
analysis.location_and_population: Global (Moderna's norovirus vaccine program). Affected population: Volunteers in the ongoing Phase 3 trial.
analysis.event: Moderna announced its Phase 3 trial of the mRNA norovirus vaccine did not achieve early success criteria. The study is continuing, with a new group of volunteers being enrolled for winter testing.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: No specific case counts or deaths reported. The setback affects Moderna's strategy to reduce reliance on Covid vaccines. The risk is limited to the program's advancement, not public health.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study is ongoing, with additional volunteers being enrolled for winter testing. Moderna emphasized the trial continues, but the early benchmark failure introduces uncertainty. The company's broader strategy depends on this and other pipeline programs.

analysis.brief_en: Moderna's norovirus vaccine program faced a setback on July 31, 2026, when the company announced its Phase 3 trial failed to meet early success criteria. Despite this, Moderna emphasized the study continues, with a new group of volunteers being enrolled for winter testing. The setback impacts Moderna's strategy to diversify beyond Covid vaccines, though the company's stock has nearly doubled this year, partly due to enthusiasm for its cancer vaccine partnership with Merck. The ongoing trial and potential winter testing remain key events for investors, as Moderna seeks to broaden its product portfolio.

supplementary_news.content_title: Cryo-EM study reveals dynamic structure of human norovirus
supplementary_news.content: Human norovirus is the leading cause of acute gastroenteritis worldwide and is estimated to infect 600–700 million people each year. Despite its enormous public health impact, no effective antiviral drugs are currently available. A detailed understanding of the three-dimensional structure of the virus is essential for elucidating its infection mechanism and developing effective therapeutics. However, research on human norovirus has been hampered by the inability to efficiently propagate the virus in cultured cells, making it difficult to obtain sufficient quantities of infectious particles for structural studies. In contrast, studies of murine norovirus, which can readily be propagated in cell culture, have shown that its capsid undergoes conformational changes in response to environmental conditions. Whether human norovirus exhibits similar structural dynamics has remained unknown. To address this question, the research team successfully produced virus-like particles (VLPs) of the human norovirus GII.3 strain, which has been responsible for repeated regional outbreaks, and determined their structures using state-of-the-art cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). Structural analysis revealed that a single VLP preparation contained two distinct conformational states, referred to as the resting and rising states, which differ in the location of the protruding (P) domain. Further analysis showed that (1) in the resting state, the P domain is positioned close to the underlying shell (S) domain and forms an extensive interaction network mediated primarily by the distal P2 subdomain. (2) In the rising state, the P domain is elevated by approximately 1 nm and rotated by about 55°, accompanied by a reorganization of the interaction network to the P1 subdomain. In addition, the P domain in the rising state exhibits substantially greater structural flexibility than in the resting state. These findings provide the first evidence that the human norovirus capsid, like that of murine norovirus, is not a rigid shell but a dynamic molecular assembly capable of adopting multiple conformations in response to its environment. Because the P domain contains both the host receptor-binding sites and the major antibody epitopes, these conformational changes may play important roles in regulating viral infectivity, receptor recognition, and immune evasion. Future studies will investigate the environmental factors-such as pH, metal ions, and physiological acids-that trigger these structural transitions, determine whether the same conformational changes as shown in murine norovirus occur in infectious virions, and explore the development of antibodies or small-molecule compounds capable of stabilizing or inhibiting these transitions. Such studies are expected to provide a foundation for the development of next-generation vaccines and novel antiviral therapies against human norovirus. Source: Journal reference: Song, C., et al. (2026). Conformational Plasticity of the Human Norovirus GII.3 Capsid Reveals Alternative P Domain Interaction Networks. International Journal of Molecular Sciences. DOI: 10.3390/ijms27156586. https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/27/15/6586
